Materials and methods
Design and physiochemical properties of the peptides
This study systematically investigated the effects of Gly capping at the N-terminus and end-tagging with single hydrophobic residues at the C-terminus on the antifungal activity of the short amphiphilic peptide W4 (RWRWWWRWR-NH
2
). The peptide design followed our previous research, as outlined below: (1) Gly, as a helix capping residue, promotes α-helical hydrogen bonding and prevents α-AMPs from losing their helicity within microbial cell. This contributes to improving the stability and activity of AMPs
[20]
. Therefore, Gly was introduced as a capping residue at the N-terminus of W4 to generate GW4; (2) End-tagging with hydrophobic amino acids, including Trp/Phe
[16]
,
[21]
, Ile
[22]
, β-naphthyl alanine
[23]
,
[24]
, is a simple and effective strategy to improve AMP stability and activity with minimal toxicity
[25]
. Consequently, hydrophobic residues, including isoleucine (I), leucine (L), alanine (A), tryptophan (W), valine (V), and phenylalanine (F), were added to the C-terminus of W4 and GW4 to produce a series of end-tagged peptides with hydrophobic residues.
The peptides were synthesized by GL Biochem Ltd. in Shanghai, China, and matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization-time-of-flight mass spectrometry conducted by Linear Scientific Inc. was used to determine their actual molecular weights, with a purity exceeding 95 % (
Figure S2
,
Table S1
). High-performance liquid chromatography was employed to further evaluate their purity. We utilized the Heli Quest analysis website (
http://heliquest.ipmc.cnrs.fr/cgi-bin/ComputParamsV2.py
) to obtain the primary structural parameters of these peptides (
Figure S1
). Subsequently, we used the online tool available at
http://rzlab.ucr.edu/scripts/wheel/wheel.cgi
to perform helical wheel projections, which provide a visual representation of the secondary structure of the peptide (
Figure S3
). We employed I-TASSER (
https://zhanglab.ccmb.med.umich.edu/I-TASSER/
) to predict and visualize the spatial arrangement of the peptides for a more comprehensive understanding of the three-dimensional structure. The secondary structures of each peptide (100 μM) were measured using 10 mM phosphate-buffered saline (PBS; pH 7.4), 50 % TFE, and 10 mM DPC micelles as previously described
[26]
.
Biocompatibility assay
The biocompatibility of the engineered peptides was evaluated following established protocols
[27]
, which involved assessing their toxicity against mouse red blood cells and two cell lines: porcine kidney (PK15) cells and HD11 macrophages.
Antifungal activity assays
MIC/MFC assay.
The antifungal activity of the peptides was evaluated using a modified version of the standardized broth microdilution method, described in Clinical and Laboratory Standardization Institute document M27-A2
[28]
. Yeast colonies were suspended in roswell park memorial institute (RPMI) 1640 growth medium (Hyclone, Thermo scientific, USA), buffered with (3-(N-morpholino) propanesulfonic acid (MOPs) (Biotopped, Beijing Biotopped, China), and diluted to a final concentration of 0.5–1 × 10
3
CFU/mL. The peptides were serially diluted in a 0.2 % albumin, bovine (BSA) (VWR Chemicals, Pennsylvania, USA) solution and mixed with the yeast suspension in equal volumes within 96-well plates. Following incubation at 30 °C for 48 h, the MIC was determined. The MIC was identified as the lowest peptide concentration capable of inhibiting 95 % of yeast cell growth. This inhibition was measured by absorbance at 492 nm using a microplate reader. Additionally, a 50 µL aliquot from each well was extracted and spread onto Yeast extract Peptone Dextrose (YPD) (Hopebio, Qingdao Hopebio, China), which were subsequently incubated at 30 °C for 48 h. The MFC was identified as the lowest peptide concentration that completely eliminated yeast cells (>99.99 % kill rate). Each experiment was conducted in triplicate, and the entire procedure was repeated thrice to ensure the reliability of the results
[29]
.
The killing kinetics assay.
The killing kinetics of the peptides against
C. albicans
cgmcc 2.2086 were further investigated. Peptides were used at a concentration equivalent to 1 × MFC. They were incubated with
C. albicans
suspensions diluted to approximately 10
3
CFU/mL with RPMI 1640-MOPs medium at various time intervals. Subsequently, 20 μL samples were extracted and plated onto Yeast Peptone Dextrose agar plates and incubated at 30 °C for 48h. The resulting colonies were counted. The reported results represent the mean values obtained from three separate experiments, ensuring the reliability and consistency of the data.
Synergy with antifungal drugs.
The checkerboard titration method is a commonly employed technique for evaluating the synergy of different combinations of antifungal drugs
[30]
. Initially, 2-fold serial dilutions of fluconazole (MackLin, Shanghai Mackli, China), ketoconazole (MackLin, Shanghai Mackli, China), amphotericin B (Beyotime, Shanghai Beyotime Biotechnology, China), and GW4 were prepared. Subsequently, 50 μL each of different concentrations of fluconazole, ketoconazole, amphotericin B and GW4 was mixed and added 100 μL of
C. albicans
cgmcc 2.2086 solution diluted to 10
3
CFU/mL with RPMI 1640-MOPs medium in the 96-well. The plates were incubated at 30 °C for 48 h. Subsequent steps followed the MIC determination method. The fractional inhibitory concentration (FIC) index (FICI) was calculated using the formula provided below:
FICI = (MIC of drug A in combination) / (MIC of drug A alone) + (MIC of drug B in combination) (MIC of drug B alone)
A FICI < 0.5 was considered synergistic; 0.5 < FICI < 1.0 was considered additive; 1.0 < FICI < 4.0 was considered indifferent, and a FICI > 4.0 was considered antagonistic.
Drug Resistance.
The drug resistance was induced by the repetitive treatment of
C. albicans
cells with antifungal drugs at sub-MIC concentrations
[27]
. A 2 mL of
C. albicans
cgmcc 2.2086 (10
6
CFU/mL) was diluted 1000-fold in RPMI 1640-MOPs medium. Subsequently, it was incubated with GW4 and fluconazole at sub-MIC concentrations in successive passages. At the end of each generation, the
C. albicans
MIC was assessed. This process was iterated for 20 generations to investigate the emergence of drug resistance.

The impact of physiological salts (including 150 mM NaCl, 4.5 mM KCl, 6 μM NH
4
Cl, 8 μM ZnCl
2
, 1 mM MgCl
2
, 2 mM CaCl
2
and 4 μM FeCl
3
) on the antifungal activity of the peptides against
C. albicans
cgmcc 2.2086 (10
3
CFU/mL; incubated at 30 °C for 48 h in RPMI 1640-MOPs medium) was evaluated to determine their salt sensitivity as previously described
[31]

Mechanism of action of the peptide
Fluorescence Imaging.
Super-resolution fluorescence microscopy and confocal laser-scanning microscopy were the initial methods used to determine the site of action of the peptide on
C. albicans
cgmcc 2.2086, utilizing fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC)-labeled peptide and propidium iodide (PI) (Biosharp, Labgi, China) staining
[32]

C. albicans
(10
6
CFU/mL) at 30 °C for 15 min. After the incubation, the
C. albicans
cells were washed thrice with PBS buffer (10 mM; pH 7.4) and resuspended (1000
g
, 10 min). Subsequently, they were incubated with 10 μg/mL PI for 15 min to identify dead or compromised cells. Excess unbound PI dye was subsequently removed by centrifugation (3000
g
, 5 min). The prepared
C. albicans
suspension was applied to a slide and secured with a coverslip. Images were captured with a Leica TCS SP2 confocal laser scanning microscope and a Delta Vision OMX 3D-SIM system, which used 488 and 535 nm bandpass filters for FITC and PI excitation, respectively. The
C. albicans
cells that were untreated with peptides served as the control group for comparison.
Cytoplasmic membrane permeabilization and depolarization assays.
The fluorescent dye NPN (N-phenyl-1-naphthylamine) (Sigma-Aldrich, Shanghai Aldrich, Germany) and the DiSC
3
-5(MKBio, Shanghai Maokang Biotechnolog, China) were used to monitor the alterations in cell wall permeabilization and the cytoplasmic membrane of
C. albicans
cgmcc 2.2086 (at 10
6
CFU/mL) after treatment with the peptide, following previously established methods
[33]

Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM).
Mid-log-phase
C. albicans
cgmcc 2.2086 cells (10
6
CFU/mL) were incubated with GW4 at 1 × MIC for 30 min in RPMI 1640-MOPs medium to prepare SEM and TEM samples. Subsequently, the cells were centrifuged at 1000
g
for 10 min, triple-fixed with PBS (10 mM, pH 7.4), and harvested. Finally, the fungal cells were fixed in a 2.5 % (
w/v
) glutaraldehyde solution at 4 °C overnight. SEM and TEM samples were prepared following previously described methods

Intracellular production of ROS was evaluated using the 2′,7′-dichlorofluorescein diacetate (DCFH-DA) (Acmec, Shanghai Acmec Biochemical Technology, China) assay, following a previously established protocol

C. albicans
cgmcc 2.2086 cells were cultured at 10
6
CFU/mL and exposed to a final concentration of 10 μM DCFH-DA at 30 °C for 1 h. The
C. albicans
cells were harvested and washed twice with 10 mM PBS (1000
g
, 10 min) to eliminate residual DCFH-DA. Subsequently, a mixture containing equal volumes of N-acetylcysteine (NAC) solution in PBS (10 mM) and
C. albicans
cell suspension was prepared, resulting in a cell density of 10
6
CFU/mL with an NAC concentration of 7.5 mM. An enzyme marker with an excitation wavelength set at 488 nm and an emission wavelength set at 530 nm was used to continuously monitor the changes in fluorescence. This experiment was independently replicated thrice to ensure consistency and reliability.

C. albicans
cgmcc 2.2086 cells (10
6
CFU/mL) were incubated with GW4 at 1 × MIC for 1 h in RPMI 1640-MOPs medium. They were initially washed twice with 10 mM PBS buffer (1000
g
, 10 min). Subsequently, they were gently resuspended using 188 µL of Annexin V-FITC. We added 2 µL of Mito-Tracker Red CMXRos, 5 µL of Annexin V-FITC, and 5 µL of Hoechst 33342 to the cell suspension and mixed gently. The
C. albicans
cells were incubated at 30 °C for 30 min in the absence of light, with intermittent resuspension performed 2–3 times during the incubation. After centrifugation at 1000
g
for 5 min, the cells were gently resuspended in 50–100 µL of Annexin V-FITC. The prepared samples were observed under a fluorescent microscope. This procedure allowed for assessing mitochondrial membrane potential and apoptosis-related markers in
C. albicans
cgmcc 2.2086 cells and was performed as per the manufacturer’s instructions.
Anti-biofilms
Biofilm formation.
Fungal suspensions of
C. albicans
cgmcc 2.2086 (OD
600nm
= 0.4) were prepared in RPMI 1640 buffered with MOPs
[36]

Inhibition of biofilm formation.
50 µL of
C. albicans
cell suspension was combined with various concentrations of 50 µL of GW4, fluconazole, or amphotericin B to reach a final volume of 100 µL per well. After 48 h of incubation at 30 °C, the well plates were gently washed with sterile PBS (10 mM, pH 7.4) to eliminate suspended and loosely adherent
C. albicans
. Following the wash, each well was incubated in the absence of light for a minimum of 4 h after adding 50 µL of methyl thiazolyl tetrazolium solution (MTT) (Merck, Shanghai Merck, China). These steps were followed by an additional 1 h incubation period. The OD
570nm
was determined by carefully transferring 85  µL from each well to a new 96-well plate. Each experiment included positive and negative controls, and the entire process was independently repeated thrice.
Elimination of pre-adhered biofilm.
The 100 μL aliquots of the
C. albicans
cell suspension were transferred into 96-well plates and incubated for 48 h, allowing for the complete development of biofilms. This served as a control group with positive results. After incubation, non-adherent
C. albicans
cells were removed by rinsing with sterile PBS (10 mM, pH 7.4). Subsequently, 100 μL of GW4, fluconazole, or amphotericin B were added to the respective wells in various concentration gradients. The plates were subsequently incubated at 30 °C for 48 h. The measurements were conducted as above described. This entire process was repeated independently thrice, with each experiment submitted in three identical copies to ensure the reliability and consistency of the results.
Live/Dead staining and fluorescence imaging of
C. albicans
biofilms.
We added 1 mL of the suspension of
C. albicans
cells in each well of a 24-well cell plate and subsequently incubated at 30 °C for 48 h to facilitate biofilm formation. After the incubation, the biofilm was washed twice with sterile 10 mM PBS buffer. Subsequently, 1 mL of GW4 (32 µM), fluconazole (2048 µM), or amphotericin B (16 µM) was added to each well and incubated at 30 °C for an additional 24 h. The biofilm was stained with SYTO-9(Thermo Fisher Scientific, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, USA) and PI after the incubation. The procedure was performed in darkness at 30 °C for 30 min. Subsequently, the dye was removed, and 500 µL of sterile PBS (10 mM, pH 7.4) was introduced. Images of the biofilm were captured using the TCS SP8 CLSM system by Leica, Germany. This comprehensive procedure was designed to evaluate the impact of GW4, fluconazole, and amphotericin B on previously established biofilms.
Quantitative real-time RT-PCR (qRT-PCR) analysis of
C. albicans
biofilm-related genes.
We evaluated the effect of GW4 on the transcript levels of genes associated with biofilm formation using qRT-PCR
[37]

C. albicans
biofilm adhering to the bottom of the culture plate was collected using a cell scraper, and the
C. albicans
cells were subsequently harvested via centrifugation (1000
g
, 10 min). Previously established protocols were employed to isolate total RNA from the
C. albicans
cells
[38]
.
Subsequently, the quality, concentration, and reverse transcription of the extracted RNA (Promega, Madison, USA) were assessed.
Table S5
illustrates the utilized primer sequences. Fluorescence quantification was performed using a 10 µL of qRT-PCR reaction system (Promega, Madison, USA). Each experiment was conducted in triplicate and the entire process was independently replicated thrice.
In vivo
assessment
In vivo
toxicity assessment.
We procured 40 female ICR mice, aged 6–8 weeks with an average weight of 20.29 ± 1.75 g, from Liaoning Changsheng Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Shenyang, China). Furthermore, all the mice were offered a 3-day adaptation period before the commencement of the experiments. The compatibility of the AFPs
in vivo
was assessed using a previously established method
[28]
, which was performed as follows: The mice were randomly divided into four groups, with 10 mice in each group (5 mice per cage). These mice were administered intraperitoneal injections of different substances, including saline, 5, 10 and 20 mg/kg GW4, every 24 h for 3 days. The condition of the mice was closely monitored, and their body weights were recorded daily throughout the period. The mice were humanely put to sleep on day four by administering excessive anesthesia. Subsequently, their serum was collected and analyzed for various parameters, including serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), total blood bilirubin (TBIL), blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and serum creatinine (CRAE). An automated biochemical analyzer from Roche Cobus Mira Plus, Switzerland, performed these measurements. Additionally, the weights of the livers, kidneys, and spleens were measured and preserved in 4 % paraformaldehyde fixative for histological examination using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining.
Establishment of the scratch keratomycosis model.
Individual colonies were separated and subsequently dissolved in the YPD medium. Subsequently, the cultures were incubated at 30 °C and 100 rpm for 16–18 h. The
C. albicans
cgmcc 2.2086 organisms were washed thrice with sterile saline and resuspended in sterile saline to achieve an optical density of 0.6 at 600 nm (OD
600nm
). We procured 40 female BALB/C mice (procured from Liaoning Changsheng Biotechnology Co., Ltd., Shenyang, China) to establish a mouse
C. albicans
-associated keratitis model. The mice received anesthesia through an intraperitoneal injection of 10 % chloral hydrate (110 µL/20 g). A 9-gauge needle was used to delicately abrade the central corneal area of the unilateral eye to damage the superficial layer of the cornea. Subsequently, the eyelid was gently pulled, and 20 µL of
C. albicans
cell liquid was included in the scratch. The ocular condition was observed after 18 h. A cornea that exhibited cloudiness, ulceration, and bulging was considered to have successfully established the keratitis model. A disease scale of 0 (no disease) to 4 (severe disease) was used to assess the effectiveness of the treatment (
Table S6
). Furthermore, all mice received subcutaneous injections of cyclophosphamide (100 mg/kg) (Aladdin, Shanghai Aladdin, China) for 3 days to induce immunosuppression.
The mice were divided into four groups, with ten mice in each group. The first group received saline, while the second and third groups received GW4 eye drops at 5 and 10 mg/mL, respectively. The fourth group received amphotericin B eye drops. Eye drops (20 μL) were instilled in each mouse every 5 min during the initial 1 h, followed by every 30 min for the next 7 h. After the final treatment, all mice were euthanized, and their eyeballs were collected immediately for analysis. A histological examination was performed on five eyeballs from each group, while the remaining five eyeballs were used for quantitative fungal recovery studies on homogenized samples. Fixed eyeballs were embedded in paraffin, sectioned, and stained using a standard Periodate-Schiff (PAS) stain protocol.
Statistical analysis
Data are presented as the mean ± standard deviation (SD) and analyzed using unpaired Student's
t
-test or a one-way ANOVA. The corresponding
P
values were reported as follows:
* P
< 0.05
, ** P
< 0.01, indicating statistical significance.
Ethics statement
The Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at Northeast Agricultural University approved the experimental protocols employed in this study. The animal welfare and treatment procedures adhered to the guidelines outlined in the “Laboratory Animal Management Regulations” (revised 2016) of Heilongjiang Province, China. All animal experiments were conducted according to the ethical policies and procedures approved by the College of Animal Science and Technology, Northeast Agricultural University, China (NEAUEC20240262).

Introduction
Immunocompromised populations, including the elderly, immunodeficient individuals, patients with severe illnesses including AIDS, cancer, diabetes, and those undergoing transplantation procedures, have heightened susceptibility to invasive fungal diseases
[1]
. Furthermore, the extensive administration of steroid medications in numerous patients with COVID-19 has significantly compromised their immune systems
[2]
, exacerbating their susceptibility to invasive fungal infections. This is illustrated by the emergence of instances of Mucormycosis caused by Mucorales in India and multidrug-resistant
Candida auris
infections in the US. These infections were associated with mortality rates as high as 60 % following the initial surge of the COVID-19 pandemic. Dissemination of these incidents has occurred in several countries, including China
[3]
,
[4]
. Unfortunately, the widespread misuse of traditional antifungal drugs has resulted in resistance, posing a significant threat to clinical infections caused by invasive fungi
[5]
. Furthermore, the development of new antifungal drugs has stagnated in recent decades. No new efficacious classes of antifungal drugs targeting invasive fungal infections have successfully emerged on the market since the introduction of caspofungin, an echinomycin-based antifungal drug, in the United States in 2004
[6]
,
[7]
,
[8]
. Most conventional antifungal drugs primarily target specific components within fungal cell membranes and inhibit their biosynthetic pathways involving ergosterol or sphingomyelin
[9]
. This limited variety of targets significantly increases the likelihood that fungi will develop multidrug resistance against multiple available antifungals. Therefore, it is imperative to conduct research aimed at discovering new antifungal drugs with new mechanisms of action to combat fungal resistance effectively.
Antifungal peptides (AFPs) are a class of small molecular peptides that are abundant in nature, synthesized by different organisms, and exhibit potent antifungal activity. They have the distinct advantages of low toxicity and decreased susceptibility to drug resistance, making them a promising alternative to conventional antifungal medications
[10]
. However, the clinical application of AFPs is hindered by their inherent limitations, including low efficacy and vulnerability to physiological conditions
[11]
. The structural optimization and modification of AFPs, guided by an understanding of structure–function relationships, have emerged as effective strategies for enhancing the clinical applicability of AFPs to overcome these challenges
[12]
,
[13]
,
[14]
,
[15]
. Regrettably, the precise description of structure–function relationships in AFPs remains unclear. Therefore, a comprehensive understanding of the structure–function relationships in AFPs is required for molecular refinement and the artificial design of cost-effective, low-toxicity, highly stable, and clinically efficacious AFPs.
In our previous study
[16]
, we systematically analyzed the therapeutic potential of peptide W4 using end-tagging with various single hydrophobic residues at the C-terminus and glycine (Gly) capped at the N-terminus. We found that the combination of Alanine (Ala) end-tagging at the C-terminal and Gly capping at the N-terminus resulted in the most potent antibacterial activity of W4. However, it is essential to recognize that fungal cell membranes, primarily composed of chitin and sterols
[17]
, significantly differ from the bacteria cell membranes
[18]
,
[19]
. Consequently, using a combination strategy involving Ala end-tagging at the C-terminal and Gly capping at the N-terminus may not be the optimal approach to improving the antifungal efficacy of W4. A systematic investigation of the effect of Gly capped at the N-terminus and end-tagging with hydrophobic residues at the C-terminals on the antifungal activity of W4 is required to address this knowledge gap. As anticipated, Gly capped at the N-terminus significantly improves the antifungal efficacy of the peptides. However, the influence of end-tagging with hydrophobic residues at the C-terminus on the antifungal activity of the peptides was limited by various factors. GW4 exhibited the highest therapeutic index (TI
GW4
= 40.99) against all 14 tested yeast species and induced yeast cell death through a multimodal action mechanism. Additionally, GW4 exhibited exceptional biocompatibility
in vivo
and a significant ability to inhibit biofilm formation and eradicate mature
Candida albicans
cgmcc 2.2086 biofilms. Importantly, GW4 exhibited outstanding efficacy against
C. albicans
-associated keratitis in mice (
Fig. 1
). This study demonstrated additional insights into the complex structure–function relationship inherent in AFPs, enhancing our evolving understanding of their functionality and establishing a theoretical basis for developing highly potent AFPs.

Designing end-tagging peptides with low toxicity, antifungal mechanisms, action on biofilms, and

efficacy. (Helical structure diagram from

We investigated whether the hydrophobic residues tagged at the C-terminal could enhance the antifungal efficacy of GW4 and W4. Incorporating different hydrophobic residues at C-terminal end-tags unexpectedly compromised the antifungal activity of GW4. However, the antifungal activity of W4 was variable due to the tagging of different hydrophobic residues at the C-terminus. Compared to unmodified W4, the average antifungal activity (GM

Our previous studies have demonstrated that the presence of hydrophobic residues at the C-termini, as indicated by end-tags, significantly impacts the average hydrophobicity values (total hydrophobicity divided by residue number) of GW4 and W4. This influence is a critical determinant of their antibacterial activity; however, ensuring that these average hydrophobicity values remain within a suitable range is essential
[16]
. Similarly, hydrophobicity plays a crucial role in the antifungal activity of AMPs. Lee et al. reported that the antifungal activity of AMPs correlates with their hydrophobicity, and intermediate levels of hydrophobicity result in high antifungal activity against

[46]
.
Herein, we have observed that hydrophobic residues at the C-terminus can modulate the antifungal activity of peptides; however, the correlation between this modulation and hydrophobicity was statistically non-significant (

The alteration in average hydrophobicity resulting from the presence of hydrophobic residues at the C-terminus may be considered one of the pivotal factors influencing the antifungal activity of peptides; however, it was crucial to consider the specific type of hydrophobic residues and the core peptide sequence as critical variables that should not be disregarded. Therefore, considering all factors comprehensively, GW4 exhibited the most potent antifungal activity (GM

The combination approach is an effective strategy for addressing the current challenge of antifungal drug resistance, given the significant distance yet to be covered before AFPs can supplant conventional antifungal drugs

The above experimental findings clarified the complex antifungal mechanism employed by the amphiphilic short peptide GW4. GW4 accumulated on the surface of microorganisms and initiated its antifungal action by penetrating the

C. albicans

Conclusions
In this comprehensive study, we systematically investigated the effect of different single hydrophobic residue end-tags and Gly capping at the N-terminal on the antifungal activity of the peptide W4 (RWRWWWR-NH
2
). We found that Gly capped at the N-terminus enhanced the helical propensity of peptides, thereby increasing their antifungal activity. However, factors including hydrophobic residue type, average hydrophobicity, and sequence composition limited the impact of C-terminal hydrophobic residue tagging on peptide antifungal activity. Additionally, we examined the influence of Gly capping at the N-terminus and end-tagging with hydrophobic residues on the antifungal activity of these engineered peptides in the presence of physiological salt concentrations. These modifications exhibited a minimal impact focused on enhancing or preserving the salt stability of these peptides under these conditions. Of particular significance, our study demonstrated the exceptional therapeutic potential of GW4, which exhibited the highest TI value (TI
GW4
= 40.99) among the examined peptides. Remarkably, GW4 demonstrated a TI value 1.90 times higher than that of W4. Mechanistically, GW4 achieved fungicidal activity by disrupting the
C. albicans
cell membrane structure, resulting in pore formation and subsequent leakage of intracellular contents. Concurrently, it aided the buildup of intracellular ROS while reducing the potential of the mitochondrial membrane. This dual mode of action, which targets both the internal and external aspects of yeast cells, indicated promise for reducing the development of resistance in microorganisms. Furthermore, our study revealed that GW4 could inhibit
C. albicans
biofilm formation and eliminate mature
C. albicans
biofilms. This activity was associated with decreased expression levels of key genes HWP1, RAS1, and TEC1, which resulted in decreased mycelial adhesion and inhibition of the
C. albicans
biofilm adhesion and virulence. In conclusion, this study demonstrated that N-terminal Gly capping and C-terminal end-tagging with hydrophobic residues significantly affect the antifungal activity of peptides, providing valuable insights for rational antifungal peptide design and optimization. These findings have significant potential to advance the development of new antifungal medications.
